newsitem.title: PERU: More Peru hostages freed after rebels meet official.
newsitem.headline: More Peru hostages freed after rebels meet official.

text.p: A first face-to-face meeting between Marxist rebels and an envoy of Peru's President Alberto Fujimori has led to the release of 20 more hostages from the Japanese ambassador's residence, leaving 83 captives on Sunday in the mined and booby-trapped building the rebels seized on Dec. 17.

As the hostage crisis entered its 12th day, there were signs of a slight easing in the hardline stances of both the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas and the government of Fujimori.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo, Fujimori's education minister, said following the release of the 20 hostages on Saturday that he had met rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini inside the building and that there had been "advances for the solution of this serious incident".
Palermo stopped short of giving the full imprimatur of the State to his talk with Cerpa, saying their conversation was "oficioso" -- a Spanish term which can mean unofficial or semi-official.
But the meeting was still a virtually unheard-of gesture from the Fujimori administration.

Fujimori himself has spoken in jail to Abimael Guzman, the captured head of the separate Shining Path rebel movement, but no official of his government has been known to speak to guerrilla leaders actively involved in hostilities.
The MRTA rebels, who took over the building in a spectacular assault on the night of Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception, also appeared to soften their position.

In a statement signed by Cerpa and read out by one of the released hostages on Saturday, the rebels omitted earlier threats to kill their prisoners if MRTA members held by the Fujimori government are not freed.

Instead they said they were willing "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue" and asked public opinion to "reflect" on the conditions under which their jailed members are being held.

"We think that this will allow it to be understood that our request should be attended to and thus permit in the long run ... a global and lasting peace," the statement said. "We will play a responsible role in that effort."
The rebels also objected to being labeled "terrorists" and angrily rejected comparisons with the Maoist Shining Path, Peru's older, more violent guerrilla group.
On Friday the Group of Seven industrial nations, in a strongly worded statement of support for Fujimori, called the rebels "terrorists", an epithet also widely used in pro-government media.

With the release of the 20 hostages on Saturday -- the ambassadors of Malaysia and the Dominican Republic, nine Japanese and one South Korean businessman, seven Peruvian diplomats and one local businessman -- the MRTA rebels had freed more than 420 of their original captives.
Fujimori has flatly rejected a guerrilla request for the release of 400 MRTA members held in Peruvian jails.
Still being held in the residence by the approximately 20 rebels were Fujimori's brother, Pedro, and several high-ranking Peruvian police and government officials.

A police source told Reuters on Saturday that three experts from the United States were in Lima helping Peruvian police analyse conversations taking place inside the residence, which were being picked up by surveillance teams using sophisticated electronic eavesdropping devices.
The source, who declined to be named, also said other U.S. experts were advising Peruvian troops preparing for a possible last-resort assault on the compound.

Since winning elections in 1990, Fujimori, who is of Japanese origin, cracked down on both the Shining Path and MRTA, sending troops to pursue them into remote jungle and mountain strongholds and capturing hundreds.

Until the Dec. 17 raid on the Japanese residence, he had claimed to have restored peace and order to Peru after years of guerrilla raids and bomb attacks. Japan has been the biggest donor of development aid to Peru since Fujimori came to power.

Still clad in the elegant but crumpled suits they wore to the Dec. 17 reception in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito, the 20 men released on Saturday left the residence in single file and, looking haggard and subdued, boarded a bus which whisked them away for medical examinations.
Scenes of joy erupted at Lima's Japanese-Peruvian Cultural Association when the 10 Japanese men freed on Saturday were reunited with their families and friends.
"Everyone was embracing and bowing, while their relatives were touching them as if to say: 'They really are here'," said Luis Tamamoto, the association's secretary general.
"They looked very happy. It was as if they had come out of prison."
